title: Should my mother sell her leasehold house before the lease gets too short?
videoTitle: ASKING SEAN #217 | SELL THE PROPERTY BECAUSE LEASEHOLD
excerpt: A mother in her 60s with three paid-off properties wants to sell a rented leasehold house before banks stop lending on it. Sean would keep it, and refinance instead if she needs cash.

qa.asker: YC, a viewer who wrote in on his mother's behalf
qa.context: YC's mother is in her 60s. She owns a single-storey leasehold house in Ampang worth about RM360,000, let for RM1,200 a month, with about 64 years left on the lease; she has heard banks are reluctant to lend once fewer than 60 years remain. She also owns a fully paid apartment and a shop lot, both rented out, and herself rents a double-storey house in OUG for convenience.
qa.question: Should she sell the house and put the money into EPF, or keep it?
qa.quote: I will never sell any property unless it's losing money.
qa.answer: Keep it. The house is paid off and its rent sustains itself, and the leasehold issue will matter more to her heirs than to her. If she wants more cash for peace of mind, refinance the apartment or shop lot only as far as their rent can repay, rather than selling an asset that pays its way.

reasons.title: A self-sustaining property has no reason to go
reasons.body: With no loan and steady rent, the house costs her nothing to hold. Sean would only sell a property that loses money, or if she truly needs the cash.

reasons.title: Leases can be extended
reasons.body: Sean says Selangor lets owners apply to renew a lease to 99 years for a fee, with conditions on a later sale, and points to a Penang building where a renewal lifted values sharply. Whether the house falls under Selangor or Kuala Lumpur decides which rules apply.

reasons.title: Refinancing beats selling for cash
reasons.body: Borrowing against the shop lot or apartment, only up to what the rent repays, releases cash at housing loan rates while she keeps the assets. Sean's example: a RM2 million shop lot renting at RM10,000 a month could free about RM1 million at her age.

reasons.title: Renting where you live is good value
reasons.body: Double-storey terraces in OUG cost about RM1.4 million to RM1.6 million, but renting one is far cheaper, and her rental income covers it.

actions: Check the title to see whether the house is under Selangor or Kuala Lumpur, and ask the land office about extending the lease.
Decide what the cash is for: safety, travel, charity or leaving more to the family.
If she needs cash, compare refinancing the apartment or shop lot with selling the house.
Keep enough insurance, such as MRTA or MLTA, on any new loan so it never passes to the family as debt.
Talk as a family about how the properties will be passed on.
qa.caveat: If she simply feels safer with money in EPF, selling isn't wrong; it just gives up a property that pays for itself. Lease renewal rules and fees vary by state and change, so confirm them with the land office.

sourceNote: Summarised from Sean's full English captions for Asking Sean #217. The quoted line is verbatim; everything else is paraphrased. Figures are as the viewer and Sean stated them in August 2023; lease extension rules vary by state.
